title: The DAG, reachability and packfiles
summary: History is a directed acyclic graph of commits. Reachability decides what log shows and what gc deletes; packfiles store it all compactly.

steps.title: History is a DAG
body: Commits point to their parents, never the other way, and a commit cannot be its own ancestor. That makes history a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG):
```text
D---E---F     (merged feature)
- Many commits can share a parent (branching).
- A merge commit has several parents (M: first parent C, second parent F).
- Nothing points forward: Git cannot cheaply ask *what are B's children?*, only *what are M's ancestors?*
Every history command is a graph walk:
| Command | Walk |
| `git log main` | everything reachable from main |
| `git log --first-parent main` | follow only first parents: the *mainline* (C, B, A plus M) |
| `git log main..feature` | reachable from feature, minus reachable from main |
| `git merge-base a b` | best common ancestor |

steps.prompt: For the graph above, which commits does `git log --first-parent --format=%s main` print? (Messages are the letters; one per line, newest first.)
steps.explain: From M, take only the first parent each time: C, then B, then A. D, E and F are reachable only through M's second parent.

steps.prompt: Is the commit reachable from `main` in the graph above?
items: The old commit you replaced with `--amend`
Commits of a branch you deleted without merging
steps.explain: Everything merged is reachable through the merge commit's second parent, so a merged branch can be deleted without losing anything. Amended-away and unmerged deleted work is reachable only from the reflog.

steps.title: Reachability and garbage collection
body: An object is **reachable** if you can get to it from a ref (branch, tag, HEAD, stash) or a reflog entry, following commit -> parents, commit -> tree, tree -> blobs and sub-trees.

Unreachable objects (from an abandoned rebase, an amended commit, a deleted branch, a blob you `git add`ed and then changed) are kept for a grace period and then removed by `git gc` (which also runs automatically now and then).
```text
git gc                      # pack objects, prune old unreachable ones
git fsck --lost-found       # list dangling commits and blobs: a last-resort rescue
git count-objects -vH       # how much is loose vs packed
> **Tip:** Even an uncommitted file you once `git add`ed exists as a blob. `git fsck --lost-found` can sometimes find it after a bad `reset --hard`.

steps.title: Loose objects and packfiles
body: A new object is first written **loose**: one zlib-compressed file at `.git/objects/ce/013625030ba8...` (first two hex characters as the folder).
Thousands of small files are slow, so `git gc` and every fetch or push use **packfiles**: `.git/objects/pack/pack-<id>.pack` with an `.idx` index.

Inside a pack, objects can be stored as **deltas**: *"this blob is that other blob, plus these changes"*. So while each commit is *logically* a full snapshot, the storage is close to *"only what changed"*, often smaller than the working tree itself.
This is also what travels over the network: `fetch` and `push` negotiate which commits the other side lacks and send a pack of just the missing objects.

steps.prompt: Why is the first `git fetch` after a teammate's push fast, even on a big repository?
options: Client and server compare which commits each has, and the server sends one pack containing only the missing objects, often as deltas
Git downloads only the files you have open
Fetch copies the whole repository each time, but compressed
Git skips history and downloads the latest snapshot only
steps.explain: Reachability again: the server walks from its tips back until it meets commits you already have.

steps.prompt: Match the tool or term to what it does.
pairs: packs objects and prunes old unreachable ones
many objects in one file, often stored as deltas
lists dangling objects you might rescue
walk only the mainline of merges

steps.title: Walk the graph, find the lost commit
prompt: `~/shop` has a merge in its history. Someone also deleted the branch `experiment` with `-D`, and its reflog has expired, so its commit is **unreachable**: no ref leads to it any more.
1. Save the subjects that `git log --first-parent` prints for `main`, one per line, in `~/answers/first-parent.txt`.
2. Find the unreachable commit with `git fsck` and bring it back as the branch `experiment`, before garbage collection deletes it.

checks.name: first-parent.txt follows main's first parents
checks.fail: `~/answers/first-parent.txt` should match `git log --first-parent --format=%s main`: the merge, then the main line only.

checks.name: experiment points at the lost commit again
checks.fail: The branch `experiment` should point at the lost commit `X: promising experiment`. `git fsck --lost-found` (or `--unreachable`) prints it as `dangling commit <id>`.

hints: `git fsck --lost-found` lists `dangling commit <id>`. `git show <id>` confirms it is the experiment.
solution: git branch experiment "$(git fsck --lost-found 2>/dev/null | awk '/dangling commit/ {print $3}')"
steps.explain: `--first-parent` follows the line a branch was developed on and skips the commits that merges brought in: the right view of `main` when every feature lands through a merge. Reachability is what garbage collection uses: anything no ref or reflog entry can reach is deleted by `git gc` after a grace period (`gc.pruneExpire`, two weeks by default). Until then, `git fsck` finds it.

steps.title: Count the objects, then pack them
prompt: `~/dedup` has three commits whose files share contents (`README` is `hi` in three places, `App.cs` goes `v1`, `v2`, `v1`).

1. Count how many **blob** objects the repository really holds, and save the number in `~/answers/blobs.txt`. List every object with `git rev-list --objects --all` and ask `git cat-file --batch-check` for each one's type.
2. Right now every object is a loose file. Pack them: afterwards `git count-objects -v` must show `count: 0` and one pack.

checks.name: blobs.txt has the real number of blobs
checks.cmd: cd ~/dedup && test "$(tr -d '[:space:]' < ~/answers/blobs.txt)" = "$(git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype)' | grep -c '^blob')"
checks.fail: `~/answers/blobs.txt` should hold the number of distinct blobs. Same content, same id: `hi` is stored once however many files hold it.

checks.name: no loose objects are left, one pack
checks.cmd: cd ~/dedup && git count-objects -v | grep -qx 'count: 0' && git count-objects -v | grep -qx 'packs: 1'
checks.fail: `git count-objects -v` should say `count: 0` and `packs: 1`. `git gc` packs the loose objects.

hints: `git rev-list --objects --all` prints every reachable object id (with a path for blobs and trees).
Pipe it into `git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype)'`, then `grep -c blob` counts them.
`git gc` packs everything; `git count-objects -vH` shows the result.
solution: git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype)' | grep -c blob > ~/answers/blobs.txt
steps.explain: Three blobs for seven file versions: identical contents are one object. Packing adds delta compression on top (similar, not identical, versions are stored as differences), which is why a repo with years of history is often smaller than one checkout. `git count-objects -vH` and `git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objectsize) %(rest)' | sort -n | tail` are how you find out what makes a repo big.
